title: Turn a humanoid's hung upper body round on its gantry hook, then keep it still and fit its back cover
instruction: Turn the body hanging from the swivel hook half a turn so its back faces you, then keep it still and press its back cover into place.
context: Robots that build robots must handle robots under assembly. Menlo Research's open-source humanoid Asimov 1 is built hanging from a gantry hook; its build guide's steps 10.6 and 10.7 read: "Turn the robot around so we can now work on the back cover." and "Take part 100_04C and put on the back of part 100_01C." On a swivel hook the body turns freely: the push that starts it loads it with momentum the hook's drag takes well over a turn to remove, so it must be stopped without a blow; and once there, any push off the swivel's axis turns it again, the cover's own press included. So the body is held still, or the cover pressed straight through the swivel's axis, while the curved cover is carried from its rest and seated on the open back within 5 mm and 5 degrees. Asimov and Menlo are the maker's names, for identification only. Here the upper body (torso, arms and head) hangs alone on a bench gantry, a stand-in for the whole robot, whose legs would not clear the table.
setup: Two YAM arms at the near edge of a table; positions are (x forward from the arm bases, y left) in cm, heights above the table. A bench gantry of 40 mm square steel: posts at y = 40 and -40 and a beam 83 cm up. Its ball-bearing swivel hook at (45, 0) carries Asimov 1's upper body by its shoulder shackles: torso shell, both arms hanging straight and the head, 18.3 kg, 71 cm from head to hands, 42 cm across the arms, yaw inertia 0.26 kg m2, centre of mass 35 cm up, hands 3 cm above the table. Its back is open: the battery bay, dark, where the cover goes. A free spin from 45 deg/s slows to 27.5 deg/s in 10 s. At the start it hangs still, facing the arms. The mark: turned 180 degrees, its back square to the arms. The back cover, Menlo part 100_04C (MJF PA12, 117 g, 330 x 241 x 98 mm, a handle bar 30 mm tall above a slot at its top), leans back 15 degrees on a foam rest shaped to the back, its foot on a ledge, at (26, -50). The arms start at their ready pose.
scoring: Scored by the effect: the turn is what brings the back within reach, and any turn that does is enough (about half a turn faces it to the arms); the heading itself is not scored. Real trial: a camera above tracks marks on the body's shoulders (yaw at 20 Hz or faster, the rate from one frame to the next); the cover's centre and turn against its place on the back are read from marks on its corners and on the shell's rim, by photo or feeler gauge. 1.0: the cover seated on the back, its centre within 5 mm and its turn within 5 degrees of its place, with the body still (under 1 deg/s), held 1 s; the trial then ends. 0.5: the same with the cover within 15 mm and 10 degrees of its place but not seated. 0 at any time: a blow (the spin slows or reverses by more than 25 deg/s within 0.1 s); a collision (it changes by more than 5 deg/s within 0.1 s while turning faster than 10 deg/s, no fingertip within 5 cm of the body); left spinning (over 20 deg/s at the end). Else 0.
fidelity: Rigid bodies at 240 Hz. The upper body is one rigid body from the maker's URDF, arms locked straight, link hulls as colliders, on a revolute swivel (friction 0.005). The cover's shape is the maker's STL; its colliders are 3 mm plates along its profile and a flat grip at the handle bar. The open back is a block in 2 cm bands set 4 mm inside the cover, not the shell's real ledges; the cover's 8 M4 bolts are left out, so a hand holds it home.
